user.headline: Describe your build. Get a floor plan you can act on.

posts.text:
The whole flat is 6 metres by 7.6.

One room to live and cook in, a sleeping alcove you walk into through an opening rather than a door, and a bath.

Small plans are less forgiving than big ones. There is no spare metre to absorb a mistake. Here the kitchen run is sized from the appliances that go in it, not guessed.

The plan and the file it was drawn from:
https://lnkd.in/e7ZAnF5h

#ArchCanvas #FloorPlans #SmallSpaces

One decision shapes this whole house: which rooms get the garden.

Here the living rooms and all three bedrooms face it. The bathroom, the laundry and the study take the street side. Nine rooms, each with its size on the drawing.

That is the kind of thing worth settling before you pay anyone. A designer can argue with a plan like this, improve it or throw it out, and all three are quicker than starting from "we want three bedrooms".

The plan and the file it was drawn from:
https://lnkd.in/eAqUn7m5

#ArchCanvas #FloorPlans #SelfBuild

A garden office: a timber studio at the end of the garden, with a meeting room, a store and a WC.

The drawing is the part to look at. Every room has its name and its size written on it, and the plan is checked before anyone sees it.

The pictures were made from that plan afterwards, to show how it could look. If a picture and the plan ever disagree, believe the plan.

I published this one whole, including the file it was drawn from. Anyone can redraw it and get the same sheet:
https://lnkd.in/eYuj8Pev

#ArchCanvas #FloorPlans #GardenOffice

Every plan from ArchCanvas comes with a list of what it could not get right.

It isn't hidden. It is written on the drawing. A plan that looks finished and isn't is worse than one that tells you where to look, and that list is exactly what to take to a professional next.

That is one of two decisions in these thirty seconds I'd defend. The other: there is no monthly fee. You pay when you keep a plan.

#ArchCanvas #FloorPlans #SelfBuild

Getting a first plan is the easy half. This minute is mostly about the other half: changing it.

In the film the request is "Widen the kitchen and move its door to the hall." You can type that, or drag a number on the drawing. The kitchen changes, the sizes update, and the rest of the house stays where it was.

When it looks right, it opens in CAD software, so a designer or draftsperson can carry on from your plan instead of starting from a blank page.

The drawing step is sped up. A real one takes two to three minutes.

#ArchCanvas #FloorPlans #HomeDesign

Two minutes, one house, start to finish.

I type what I want in plain English. A floor plan with real dimensions comes back. Then I change it by saying what's wrong with it.

There is one place where the film cheats, and it says so on screen: the wait. A real plan takes two to three minutes to arrive and nobody wants to watch that, so the drawing part is sped up.

The second half is four different homes. The words on screen are the actual briefs that produced them.

What you get is a first plan to take to a designer or draftsperson. It is not something to build from.

The film itself is the ArchCanvas screen rebuilt in code, not a screen recording.

#ArchCanvas #FloorPlans #SelfBuild

Curved walls are where a lot of drawing software quietly cheats. You get a many-sided polygon that looks smooth until you zoom in.

So I tested ours on the most famous curved room I could think of: the Oval Office.

This is the first floor of the West Wing, drawn with the engine underneath ArchCanvas. The bow is a real arc with a 7.3 m radius, not a row of short straight lines, and the three south windows sit at even quarters along the curve. 24 rooms, 1,569 m², one A1 sheet.

Why this matters if you are planning a house: a bay window, a curved garden wall or a round snug should come out with real sizes a builder can set out, not an approximation.

An original illustration based on publicly available floor plans. It is not an official record: the room names and the layout are the documented ones, the dimensions are plausible rather than surveyed.

The drawing and my notes: https://lnkd.in/ewrEPU-j

#ArchCanvas #FloorPlans #Architecture

media.alt: ArchLang cover card reading 'The Oval Office is an arc.' Beside it, the compiled Oval Office plan with its curved south wall, and the one-line arc source printed below it.

The West Wing first-floor plan with three callouts: the Oval Office bow drawn as one arc clause, the Cabinet Room's table and fourteen chairs from a single loop, and the windowless Roosevelt Room at the centre of the plan.
The clean compiled floor plan: 24 named and dimensioned rooms in three bands, a numbered grid, a north arrow and a title block, with the Oval Office bowing out at the lower right.

posts.text:
Most AI floor plans look right at a glance.

Then a wall stops a few centimetres short. A door is drawn too narrow. The room sizes don't quite add up. The picture looked fine. The plan underneath didn't hold.

I'm Chan Meng, and I build ArchCanvas on my own in Auckland. You describe the home you want in plain English and it designs one floor plan with real dimensions: walls that close, sizes that add up. Then you change it until it's right.

One plan, not five, is a deliberate bet. I think one consistent plan you can keep shaping for free beats several rough ones you choose between blind. If that's the wrong bet for you, the free tier costs nothing to find out.

Two things you should know before you try it:
• A plan takes about 100 to 160 seconds, because the geometry is checked before you see it.
• What you get is a first plan to take to a designer or draftsperson. It is not a stamped permit set. It makes the architect's bill smaller; it doesn't replace the architect.

No subscription. You pay for a result you keep, and credits don't expire.
